"And as the woman comes to the end of Aphrodite, she is wont to pant from the fiery pleasure, and the panting, with its amorous breath, leaping up to the lips of the mouth, meets the wandering kiss as it seeks to go down below;

"and the kiss, turning back with the panting and mingled with it, follows and strikes the heart; and the heart, stirred by the kiss, throbs. And were it not bound to the inward parts, it would have followed, drawn up by the kisses. But the kisses of boys are untaught, their embraces unschooled, their Aphrodite idle, their pleasure nothing."
And Menelaus said, "But you seem to me to be no novice, but an old hand at Aphrodite; such a flood of women's subtleties you have poured over us. Now hear in your turn the case for boys.

"In a woman everything is counterfeit, both her words and her looks; and if she seems to be beautiful, it is the elaborate device of unguents; her beauty is of perfumes, or of dyed hair, or even of kisses. But if you strip her of these many wiles, she is like the jackdaw of the fable stripped of its feathers.
"But the beauty of a boy is not watered by the scents of perfumes nor by deceitful and alien odours; and the sweat of boys smells sweeter than all a woman's unguents.

"It is permitted them, even before the embrace of Aphrodite, to come together in the wrestling-school and to clasp one another openly, and the embraces bring no shame, and no softness of flesh weakens the embraces of Aphrodite, but the bodies meet hard against one another and contend for pleasure.

"And his kisses have no womanish craft nor work any wanton deceit upon the lips, but he kisses as he knows how, and the kisses are not of art but of nature. This is the image of a boy's kiss: if nectar were congealed and became a lip, you would have such kisses. And kissing him you could have no satiety, but the more you are filled, the more you thirst still to kiss, and you could not draw your mouth away, until for very pleasure you fled the kisses."
